title: No Other Gospel: Paul's Call Came from Christ
summary: Paul greets the churches of Galatia as an apostle sent by Jesus Christ and God the Father, then, without his usual thanksgiving, expresses astonishment that they are deserting the one who called them for a different gospel, and pronounces a curse on anyone who preaches one. He begins his defense by telling how he received his gospel: by revelation from Jesus Christ, after a life of zealous persecution of the church, and not from the apostles in Jerusalem, whom he met only briefly years later.
story: Paul had brought the message of Jesus to the Galatians, and they had received it gladly (4:13-15). Since he left, teachers have arrived telling these mostly Gentile believers that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. Word of it has reached Paul, and this chapter is his first response. It sets the terms for the whole letter: there is one gospel, it came from God and not from any human authority, and adding to it means leaving it. The autobiography that begins at verse 11 runs through the end of chapter 2 and builds to the letter's central statement about justification by faith (2:15-21).
historical:
Paul's account here is one of the earliest pieces of Christian autobiography, and it overlaps with the story told in Acts 9. Before his conversion, Paul (also called Saul) had been a Pharisee, a member of a lay movement devoted to careful observance of the law and the traditions that interpreted it, and he had tried to destroy the church (Acts 8:3; 9:1-2; Philippians 3:5-6). His encounter with the risen Jesus near Damascus, usually dated to the early or mid-30s AD, turned him from persecutor to preacher.

Galatians adds details Acts does not give. Paul went away into Arabia, which here most likely means the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Damascus, whose king Aretas IV later tried to have Paul arrested (2 Corinthians 11:32). What he did there, whether preaching, reflecting, or both, the text doesn't say. After three years (by ancient counting, possibly part of the first and third years) he went up to Jerusalem to see Cephas (the Aramaic form of Peter's name) and stayed fifteen days, meeting also James, the Lord's brother, who became a leader of the Jerusalem church. Then he went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia, where his hometown of Tarsus lay (Acts 9:30). Acts compresses these years and says Barnabas brought Paul to "the apostles" (Acts 9:27); Paul's sworn statement in verse 20 that he saw only Peter and James is the more precise account from the man himself, and the two can be reconciled if Luke's phrase is general.
cultural:
Letters in the Greek and Roman world followed a set pattern: the sender's name, the recipients, a greeting, and usually a thanksgiving or prayer for the readers. Paul always adapts this form, and in every other letter he gives thanks for his readers or blesses God. In Galatians the thanksgiving is simply missing. Where it should stand, verse 6 reads, "I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you". Ancient letter writers sometimes used the language of astonishment to rebuke, and the first hearers, listening as the letter was read aloud in their assembly, would have noticed the omission at once.

Paul's description of himself draws on Jewish ideals. Zeal for the law had a long heroic tradition, from Phinehas (Numbers 25) to the Maccabees, who had fought foreign rulers in the second century BC to defend the law and the temple. Paul says he was "extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers" (verse 14), and it was that zeal that drove him to persecute the church. His language about his call also echoes the prophets: God "set me apart from my mother's womb" recalls Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1, where the servant of the Lord is called from the womb to be a light to the nations. The curse formula, anathema, also had a Jewish background, described below.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-10 are the opening of the letter, expanded to announce its theme. Even the greeting argues: Paul's apostleship is "not from men nor by man" (verse 1), and Christ "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age" (verse 4), a phrase that frames the whole debate in terms of two ages, the old and the new that Christ has opened. The rebuke of verses 6-9 repeats its curse twice for emphasis. Verses 11-12 then state a thesis (the gospel was received by revelation, not from any person), and verses 13-24 prove it by narrative, marked by time words: "when", "after three years", "later". Each step shows how little contact Paul had with Jerusalem. The oath in verse 20 shows how seriously he takes the charge that his gospel was secondhand.

outline.t: Greeting: an apostle sent by Christ, who gave himself for our sins
Astonishment and a curse on any other gospel
The gospel came by revelation from Jesus Christ
From persecutor to preacher to the Gentiles
A short visit to Jerusalem and years in Syria and Cilicia

doctrines.note: Paul insists his gospel was not devised by any human being but received "by revelation from Jesus Christ" (verse 12). The message has its source in God, which is why no apostle, angel, or teacher may change it.

The greeting compresses the gospel into one clause: Christ "gave Himself for our sins" (verse 4). His death was self-giving and it dealt with sin, and its purpose was rescue from the present evil age, the world order ruled by sin and death.

God called the Galatians "by the grace of Christ" (verse 6) and called Paul "by His grace" (verse 15). Salvation begins with God's initiative, not with human achievement; Paul's own story, a zealous persecutor stopped in his tracks, is the proof.

words.note: Euangelion, gospel or good news. In the Greek world the word could announce a victory or the birth or accession of a ruler; in Isaiah's Greek translation the related verb announces God's coming reign (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7). Paul uses it for the message about Jesus. His point in this chapter is that there is only one: a different gospel "is not even a gospel" (verse 7).

Anathema, something devoted, here a curse. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew herem, something handed over to God for destruction. Paul invokes it on anyone, himself or an angel included, who preaches a gospel contrary to the one the Galatians received (verses 8-9). It is a solemn handing over of the false teacher to God's judgment, not a personal insult.

Apokalypsis, revelation, an uncovering. The word gives the Book of Revelation its Greek title. Paul uses it for the moment God showed him who Jesus is (verse 12), and the related verb in verse 16 says God was pleased "to reveal His Son in me". His gospel came from an unveiling, not from instruction.

Zelotes, a zealot, one full of zeal. It can simply mean an enthusiast, but in Jewish usage zeal for the law carried the memory of Phinehas and the Maccabees, who used force against those who broke the covenant. Paul describes his old self this way (verse 14) to explain why he persecuted the church.

christ: In a short space the chapter says a great deal about who Christ is. He stands with God the Father as the source of Paul's apostleship, on the divine side of the line Paul draws between God and "men" (verse 1). God raised him from the dead (verse 1). He gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age (verse 4), so his death is the hinge between the old age and the new. He is the Son whom God revealed to Paul (verse 16), and grace and peace come from him together with the Father (verse 3). Paul's own life shows the gospel's power: a man who tried to destroy the church came to preach "the faith he once tried to destroy" (verse 23), and the churches of Judea glorified God because of him.

hard.q: Isn't it harsh for Paul to curse other Christian teachers over what looks like a disagreement about religious practice?
hard.a:
To a modern reader, the curse of verses 8-9 can sound like intolerance, and the dispute about circumcision can look minor. Paul did not think it was minor. In his view, requiring Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law in order to belong to God's people meant saying that Christ's death was not enough, which is why he later writes that if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing (2:21). The question was not a matter of custom but of what saves.

Three things soften the charge of mere harshness. First, Paul includes himself: "even if we or an angel from heaven" should preach another gospel. The curse falls on a message, whoever carries it, not on a rival party. Second, anathema hands the matter to God's judgment rather than authorizing anyone to punish the teachers. Third, Paul elsewhere shows great patience with believers who differ on food and holy days (Romans 14), as long as those practices are not made conditions of belonging to Christ. The line he draws here is at the gospel itself. Christians still debate where exactly that line falls in later disputes, but Paul's principle is that first-order matters deserve this seriousness and second-order ones do not.

questions: Paul says the Galatians are turning to a gospel that adds something to Christ. What do people today most often add to Christ as a condition of truly belonging to God?
Paul admits that he once violently opposed the church. What does it mean that God called him by grace at the height of that zeal?
Verse 10 asks whether Paul is seeking the approval of people or of God. Where does the desire for approval most shape what you say you believe?
